section.title: Four Chariots
section.sectionRationale: The eighth and final night vision closes the set where the first opened. Four chariots with colored horses come out from between two bronze mountains, sent as the four winds of heaven to patrol the whole earth. They carry out God's sovereign rule over the nations, and those going north bring rest to God's Spirit, signaling that judgment on Babylon is complete and God's people can be at peace.
section.thesis: The God who commands the four winds of heaven rules every direction of the earth from His heavenly court; His agents patrol the nations and execute His judgment, so that His Spirit finds rest and His people can rest in His sovereign control of history.
section.frameNote: One movement: the four chariots emerging from between the bronze mountains, their identity as the four spirits of heaven sent to patrol the earth, and the word that those going north have given rest to God's Spirit.

units.label: The four chariots patrol the earth

verses.text: And again I lifted up my eyes and saw four chariots coming out from between two mountains, mountains of {{nechosheth|bronze}}.
The first chariot had red horses, the second black horses,
the third white horses, and the fourth dappled horses, all of them strong.
So I inquired of the angel who was speaking with me, “What are these, my lord?”
And the angel told me, “These are the four {{ruach|spirits}} of heaven, going forth from their station before the Lord of all the earth.
The one with the black horses is going toward the land of the {{tsafon|north}}, the one with the white horses toward the west, and the one with the dappled horses toward the south.”
As the strong horses went out, they were eager to go and patrol the earth; and the LORD said, “Go and patrol the earth.” So they patrolled the earth.
Then the LORD summoned me and said, “Behold, those going to the land of the north have given rest to My Spirit in the land of the north.”

nechosheth.gloss: Bronze or copper, a hard and enduring metal often associated in Scripture with strength and with judgment. The two mountains of bronze form a fixed gateway from the heavenly realm, immovable and unbreakable, from which God's judgment chariots issue. Some see here the mountains flanking the LORD's dwelling, a bronze threshold between heaven and earth.

ruach.gloss: Spirit, wind, or breath. The same word names the four spirits of heaven sent out as chariots and the Spirit of God given rest in verse eight. The chariots are the winds of heaven, God's mobile agents in every direction, and their work brings rest to His Spirit, so the word frames the vision from the winds that go out to the Spirit that is stilled.

tsafon.gloss: The north, the direction from which invading armies, especially Babylon, historically swept down on Judah. In the prophets the north is the land of the great enemy and of exile. When the chariots to the north give rest to God's Spirit, it signals that judgment on the northern oppressor is accomplished and the threat to God's people is settled.

basic.context: This is the eighth and last night vision, and it matches the first. In the opening vision, riders patrolled the earth and reported it at rest under the nations. Now four chariots with colored horses come out from between two bronze mountains, sent as the four winds of heaven from God's presence to patrol the earth in every direction. The climax comes when those going north give rest to God's Spirit: the great enemy in the north, Babylon, has been dealt with, and God's rule is settled.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a symbolic vision that frames the whole set. The chariots are God's agents carrying out His will over the nations. The colors and directions signal His comprehensive rule; the details of each color matter less than the whole picture of God controlling world history. The key line is verse eight: God's Spirit is given rest, meaning His purposes against the oppressor are accomplished.
basic.originalLanguages: The chariots come from between mountains of nechosheth, bronze, an enduring metal of strength and judgment, forming a fixed gateway from heaven. The angel calls them the four ruach of heaven, the four winds or spirits, and the same word names the Spirit of God given rest in verse eight. They fan out especially to the tsafon, the north, the land of Babylon and of exile, and there God's Spirit finds rest.
basic.typology: The heavenly chariots patrolling the earth point to God's sovereign, angelic government of history, taken up in Revelation's horsemen who ride out over the earth. The rest given to God's Spirit anticipates the rest Christ secures for His people when every enemy is subdued under His feet.
basic.christ: These chariots go out from the Lord of all the earth, and the whole vision proclaims that history is governed from God's throne. In the New Testament that throne is shared by the risen Christ, to whom all authority in heaven and on earth is given, who rules the nations and will subdue every enemy. The rest given to God's Spirit foreshadows the peace Christ wins by His finished work.
basic.god: God is the Lord of all the earth, ruling every direction from His heavenly court. Nothing happens among the nations outside His command; His agents go only where He sends them. He is a God who acts in judgment on His people's oppressors, and who is satisfied, His Spirit given rest, when His righteous purposes are accomplished.
basic.crossReferences: Zechariah 1 opens with patrolling riders, matching this closing vision. Revelation 6 sends out colored horses over the earth. Psalm 103 and Daniel 7 show God's angelic host serving His rule. Matthew 28 gives all authority to the risen Christ.
basic.oneStory: The night visions close with God's chariots patrolling the whole earth and His Spirit given rest as the great enemy is judged. This declares that world history runs under God's throne, a rule now shared by the risen Christ, and it points toward the final rest when every enemy is subdued and God's people dwell in peace.

context.literary:
Chapter 6 begins with the same phrase that opens 5:1 and 5:9, 'I lifted up my eyes and saw,' and the 'again' in 6:1 tells the reader that the night's seeing is still going on, though this is the last image. The scene is bound to the first vision by echoes of vocabulary. In 1:8-11 horses of several colours stand among myrtle trees in a hollow and report that they have 'patrolled the earth.' In 6:1-8 horses of four colours come out from between two mountains and 'patrol the earth.' The verb is the same walking-to-and-fro verb in both, in a reflexive form that suggests ranging back and forth. In the first vision the news was 'all the earth is at rest and tranquil,' which God answered with fierce anger at nations that were at ease, 1:11-15. In the last the rest is a different one: it is God's Spirit who is at rest, 6:8.

Several details mark a difference between the two scenes. In the first vision the horses carry riders; in the eighth they pull chariots, and no one drives them. The angel in the first scene reports what is already done; in the eighth the LORD himself speaks the command, 'Go and patrol the earth,' and the horses go. The first is set in a shaded valley among myrtles, a place of hiddenness; the last is a gateway of bronze. What was a report at the start of the night is now an order, and what was an uncertain peace has become an accomplished purpose.

The oracle also has an odd shape. The angel names four chariots and four colours, but then gives directions for only three teams, 6:6, and the BSB footnote notes that the white horses go 'after them.' The first chariot's destination is never stated, and the section ends not with the full tour but with a single remark about the north. The omission steers the reader's attention to the one direction that matters most to the exiles. Verse 8 is then the closing line of the vision cycle, and with it the night visions end, and the prophet moves straight on, in 6:9, to the sign-act of the crown.
context.historical:
The eight visions fell in the second year of Darius, 519 BC, five months after the work on the temple had started again under Haggai's preaching, Haggai 1:1-2. The first vision had found the empire at ease. Within memory the Persians had moved through a period of revolts, and Darius had spent his first years putting down rebellions across the empire. To the exiles that meant that the great powers were shaken but not yet judged. The earlier vision had been followed by God's anger against nations 'that are at ease,' Zechariah 1:15, who had added to the calamity of his people. The question that hung over the community was whether the God who had once used Babylon was still in control of the powers that now ruled them.

The north was a loaded word. Babylon was due east of Judah, but because the desert lay between, its armies came into Canaan from the north. Jeremiah heard God say, 'Disaster from the north will be poured out on all who live in the land,' Jeremiah 1:14, and the prophets constantly spoke of Babylon as the foe from the north. Zechariah 2:6 had called the exiles to 'flee from the land of the north,' and the same verse said God had scattered them 'like the four winds of heaven,' the same image of four directions and four winds that appears here. So when the chariot with black horses goes north, the hearers would have taken it as a visit to Babylon and its territories.

Chariots also spoke of power. They were the weapon of empires, Jeremiah 4:13, and Scripture often pictures the heavenly host in chariots, Psalm 68:17 and 2 Kings 6:17. A people living under a foreign king whose power rested on cavalry and chariots needed to hear that heaven also had its chariots, and that the Lord of all the earth was not outnumbered.
context.canonical:
The vision belongs to a long series of passages in which the host of heaven goes out to carry out God's will. In Job 1:6-7 the sons of God 'come to present themselves before the LORD,' and Satan reports he has been 'roaming through the earth.' The verb for presenting themselves there is the one behind the 'station' of Zechariah 6:5, and the sense of ranging over the earth is the same. In Psalm 104:4 God 'makes the winds His messengers,' and Hebrews 1:7 quotes the line to say that angels are 'winds' and 'flames of fire.' Zechariah's four spirits, whom a footnote allows to be four winds, sit in the middle of that tradition.

The chariots of fire are another thread. Elisha's servant sees them in 2 Kings 6:17 when his eyes are opened to what always surrounds God's people. Ezekiel's vision of the throne is full of wheels and living creatures, and Daniel 7:9-10 sees thousands upon thousands serving before the Ancient of Days. Revelation 6:1-8 sends out four horses, white, red, black and pale green, when the Lamb opens the first four seals. The colours and the number connect the two visions, but Revelation's horsemen carry bow, sword, scales and death, and are given authority over a fourth of the earth, so they cannot simply be equated with Zechariah's chariots.

Finally, the title 'Lord of all the earth' is a deliberate echo. It is used in Joshua 3:11 when the ark of the covenant goes into the Jordan, and in Zechariah 4:14 of the two anointed ones. At the end of the book the claim will be put in its fullest form: 'the LORD will become King over all the earth,' Zechariah 14:9. In the New Testament it is Christ who says, 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me,' Matthew 28:18, so that the lordship over the whole earth that Zechariah ascribes to the LORD is exercised by the risen Son.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The vision gave the returned exiles a different view of the world than the one they could see. From Jerusalem the empire looked like the one in charge, and God's activity looked invisible. Zechariah meant them to see the same events from the other side of the sky. Four chariots stand at God's gate, wait on his order, and go where he says. The prophet was not offering a timetable or a map of the nations. He was offering a reason to keep building a temple in a small province: the God they served commanded the same winds that moved empires.

The final line was meant to console. When the LORD says that those going north have given rest to his Spirit, he speaks of something finished. The Spirit has been grieved and unsettled by the north's treatment of his people, and now that grief has been answered. Zechariah wanted the community to hear that the account with Babylon was closed and that they did not need to take up a quarrel that God had already settled. He also meant them to see that this rest was not a pause between wars but a settled achievement. A people who had lived for seventy years in a world that did not seem to answer for its violence were being told that it had been answered.

The hearers were also meant to notice the obedience of the horses. They are 'eager to go,' and they go the moment they are told. It is a picture for the community that the work of God does not wait on anyone's readiness, while the people are called to be as ready.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The vision describes what is true of heaven. It does not command the reader to imitate the chariots, to calculate directions, or to assign a nation to each colour. Efforts to map the four teams onto four empires or four historical periods go beyond what the text says, and the text itself leaves out the destination of the red team. The prescriptive weight lies elsewhere: it is in the command 'Go and patrol the earth,' which is addressed to the horses and not to us.

What the vision does ask of its hearers is trust that is expressed in work. The visions in this part of the book repeatedly end in a call to build, to repent, to be honest in the market. Believing that heaven governs the earth does not excuse anyone from acting well in the part of it they occupy. The enduring truths are that God's rule is complete, that his agents obey him, and that rest for his people comes from his finished purposes and not from their own anxious management of events.

debates.question: What are the two mountains of bronze?

views.label: A heavenly gateway
views.case: The mountains look like the pillars of a gate through which the chariots go out from God's presence, as verse 5 implies with 'from their station before the Lord of all the earth.' Bronze suggests permanence and strength, and the whole scene may be a symbol, not a map. This is the safest reading because the text gives no names.

views.label: Jerusalem's own hills
views.case: Some link the two mountains to Zion and the Mount of Olives, with the valley between as the place of God's coming, because the book ends there, Zechariah 14:4-5. They note that 'again' in 6:1 returns the prophet to the earth-bound scene of the first vision. The text does not say so, and the connection would be a later reading back.

views.label: An echo of the temple's bronze pillars
views.case: The temple had two great pillars of bronze, 1 Kings 7:15-16, in front of the sanctuary. Some propose that the gateway of bronze is a heavenly version of those pillars, so that the chariots go out from the true temple. It is a suggestive link in the vocabulary, but the pillars are not called mountains.

debates.bearing: All three agree that the chariots come from God's own presence and go out under his command. None of them is needed for the point of the vision, and a reader should hold the identification loosely.

debates.question: Are the four 'spirits of heaven' angels or winds?

views.label: Angelic beings
views.case: The BSB reads 'spirits,' and elsewhere the Bible calls angels spirits and winds in the same breath, Psalm 104:4 and Hebrews 1:7. The four have a station before the Lord, they are sent, and they report. That is the language of heavenly servants.

views.label: The four winds of heaven
views.case: The BSB footnote says the word may be 'winds.' Zechariah 2:6 spoke of Israel scattered 'like the four winds of heaven,' and the chariots go to the four directions. Winds are God's messengers and instruments, and a chariot fits the idea of a wind that rushes through the land.

debates.bearing: In Hebrew thinking the two ideas overlap, and the text is happy to leave both in play. Either way, these are forces and servants entirely at God's disposal, which is the claim the vision makes.

debates.question: What do the horse colours and their directions mean?

views.label: Distinct missions of judgment
views.case: The colours may mark different kinds of divine action, as they do in Revelation 6, where red goes with war and black with famine. The three named directions would then be three fields of work in different parts of the world.

views.label: A comprehensive picture without a code
views.case: The prophet does not decode a single colour. The angel moves directly to the directions, and the interest of the passage is the north. On this reading the colours give variety and life to the picture of a complete patrol, and the effort to assign each one a meaning goes beyond the text.

debates.bearing: The second reading respects the way the angel explains the vision. The colours are not interpreted in the text, so any meaning given to them should be held lightly. The point of all four is complete reach under the one command.

study.originalLanguages:
The central verb of the vision is the one translated 'patrol.' In 1:10-11 and 6:7 it is a reflexive form of the verb for walking, which means to walk about or to range back and forth. The same form appears in Job 1:7 and 2:2, where Satan answers God that he has been 'walking back and forth' on the earth. It describes an inspection and a presence, not a march. The chariots do not conquer anything on this tour. They go through the earth the way an overseer goes through an estate, which fits the final remark that what they find is settled.

The angel names the teams 'the four spirits of heaven,' and the word for spirit is ruach, a word that also means wind and breath. The footnote at 6:5 offers 'winds.' The word recurs in a key spot: the LORD says that those going north 'have given rest to My Spirit,' and in Hebrew it is the same word again, ruach. The wordplay runs through the passage. The four ruach go out, and one result is rest for the one Ruach. The 'station' from which they go is a form of the verb for taking one's stand or presenting oneself, the verb used in Job 1:6 of the sons of God presenting themselves before the LORD. They are standing servants who stand again before they go.

The title the angel gives God, 'Lord of all the earth,' is adon, the word for master or lord, with a term for the whole earth. It is not the covenant name. The BSB names the LORD as the one who gives the order in 6:7 and summons the prophet in 6:8, though the Hebrew there simply says 'he said,' so the speaker is the one the angel has just called Lord of all the earth. The two titles are meant to be heard together: the Lord whose rule reaches every nation is the LORD who speaks to Israel. The same two names will be fused at the end of the book, where the LORD becomes king over all the earth, 14:9.

The rest in verse 8 deserves attention. The verb is a causative form of nuach, 'to rest' or 'to set down,' so God's Spirit has been caused to rest or to settle. The same verb in this causative form is used of God's anger when it is spent. In Ezekiel 5:13 he says, 'when My anger is spent and I have vented My wrath against them, I will be appeased,' and in 16:42, 'I will lay to rest My wrath against you.' The word ruach can also mean temper or anger, so some take the line as 'they have appeased My wrath in the land of the north.' The verse can carry both senses, a Spirit who is at rest and a wrath that is satisfied, and the translation 'Spirit' keeps both open.

Last, the colours. The first three are common words, adom, shachor and lavan, red, black and white. The fourth, barod, is rare. Elsewhere it describes the speckled animals in Jacob's flocks, Genesis 31:10 and 31:12, so 'dappled' or 'speckled' is a fair rendering. The first vision's horses were red, sorrel and white, 1:8, so the palette shifts. The stronger point is the noun 'strong.' The adjective is repeated in verses 3 and 7, framing the scene, so the horses are strong and eager before they move and strong when they go.

typology.type: The chariots patrolling at God's command
typology.fulfillment: The heavenly host serving the Lord of all the earth is the pattern behind every New Testament picture of angels sent out. Hebrews 1:14 calls them ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation, and Hebrews 1:7 quotes the line that makes them winds and flames. The correspondence in Christ is that he is the Lord they serve, with 'all authority in heaven and on earth,' Matthew 28:18, and with angels, authorities and powers subject to him, 1 Peter 3:22. The escalation is that the commander is no longer only enthroned but has been through death. The type falls short in that the chariots carry out a single tour and then rest, while Christ's reign continues until he has put every enemy under his feet, 1 Corinthians 15:25.

typology.type: Rest for God's Spirit in the north
typology.fulfillment: The rest given to God's Spirit after judgment on the oppressor pictures a conflict brought to its end. In Christ the greater rest is announced: 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest,' Matthew 11:28. Hebrews 4:9-10 speaks of 'a Sabbath rest for the people of God' for those who enter his rest. The escalation is that God's own satisfaction is joined to the rest of his people, because the work was finished at the cross, Hebrews 10:12-14. The type falls short because it records a rest from judging one empire, while the rest of Christ is from sin and condemnation for people from every nation.

typology.type: The four directions of the earth
typology.fulfillment: Four teams to four quarters is a picture of universal reach. The corresponding movement in the gospel is the going out of the word to all nations. Christ sends his people 'to the ends of the earth,' Acts 1:8, and in Revelation 5:9 the redeemed are purchased 'from every tribe and tongue and people and nation.' The escalation is that the reach of God's governance becomes a reach of his mercy. Zechariah 2:6 already pictured Israel scattered like the four winds of heaven, and the gathering that answers it in the New Testament is the gathering of the nations to Christ, John 12:32. The type falls short in that it describes God's lordship over the nations, not the invitation of the gospel, so it must not be pushed to say what it does not.

study.christ:
The vision does not name a Messiah, and nothing in it should be forced into a prediction. Its link to Christ is by theme and by what follows it. The theme is lordship. The angel's title, 'the Lord of all the earth,' belongs in the Old Testament to the LORD alone, and the claim of the New Testament is that the one who holds it is Jesus. When he says, 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me,' Matthew 28:18, he assumes the position that Zechariah's chariots serve. Paul says that God seated him far above every rule and authority, power and dominion, Ephesians 1:20-22, and Peter that angels, authorities and powers have been made subject to him, 1 Peter 3:22.

What follows the vision confirms the link. The next paragraph, Zechariah 6:9-15, crowns Joshua and speaks of a man called the Branch who 'will sit on His throne and rule' and 'be a priest on His throne.' The patrolling chariots have established that the whole earth is under one throne. Then the Branch is shown on it. In that sequence the first reading is of a God who rules the nations, and the second is of a Mediator who rules them as a priest. The Gospel account of Christ as both King and Priest takes the two together.

A second link is rest. The grief of the Spirit in the north is quieted when the work against the oppressor is done. In Christ the Spirit's rest becomes public. At the Jordan the Spirit descends and remains on him, John 1:32. The anger of God against sin was spent at the cross, where Jesus bore it, and Hebrews says that after offering one sacrifice for sins he 'sat down at the right hand of God,' Hebrews 10:12. Sitting is the posture of finished work. Zechariah's rest, ruach given rest, thus looks forward to the day when the Son sits down because there is no more sacrifice to offer.

A third link is the opposite of the first vision's false rest. The nations in 1:11 were at ease because they did not know God was moving. Isaiah says the wicked have no peace, Isaiah 57:20-21, and Christ is the peace that is not an absence of judgment but the settlement of it, Ephesians 2:14-16. Where the world sees tranquility as a lack of trouble, the gospel finds it in a finished reconciliation.

The chariots also stand opposite another pair of horsemen in the New Testament. The rider on a white horse in Revelation 19:11 is called Faithful and True, and he judges with justice. The vision does not predict that scene, but the idea of a judge who is perfectly in command of every quarter of the earth is the same idea in its fullest form. We read Zechariah's chariots as an early light on a truth that is only complete in him.
study.god:
This vision gives the clearest statement of God's rule over history in the book. The title 'Lord of all the earth' makes three claims at once: that God is the Lord, that he is Lord of every land, and that his lordship is exercised personally. He does not delegate his governance to the chariots and withdraw; in 6:7 it is the LORD who says 'Go,' and in 6:8 it is the LORD who summons the prophet to hear the outcome. What the empires seemed to do by their own power, he is shown doing through his agents.

The vision also shows the character of that rule. It is ordered. The chariots come from a fixed gate, go to named places, and return their report. It is responsive: the first vision's report of ease was met with anger, and the last answers it with action. And it is sufficient: the horses are strong and eager, and nothing in the account suggests resistance or delay. God does not struggle to bring his purpose about. This is the God who 'makes the winds His messengers,' Psalm 104:4, and who has 'tens of thousands' of chariots, Psalm 68:17.

There is an unexpected tenderness in verse 8. The vision of cosmic power ends on a thought about God's Spirit being at rest. The Lord of all the earth is not only an impersonal ruler. He can be unsettled by the treatment of his people and satisfied when it is answered. That is the language of a God who is personally involved and not merely administering. It balances the picture of sovereignty with one of care. His rest in the north is the quiet of a Father who has seen justice done for his children.

The passage also holds a tension. God is sovereign over the nations, yet the nations are accountable for what they do, and the vision does not say that the empire's cruelty was good because he used it. The anger of 1:15 was against nations that 'added to the calamity.' Sovereignty and responsibility sit together here as they do throughout Scripture, and the vision refuses to resolve them in a way that would make either one smaller.

For worship, the vision calls for a settled confidence. A congregation that believes the Lord of all the earth rules every direction can pray for rulers without fear and obey without despair. It can sing 'The LORD reigns' while the newspaper reports unrest. And it can also learn to wait, because the vision does not give a date for the end of every conflict. The north was dealt with at the right time, by the right command, and the people who built a temple in the meantime were not wasting their effort.

crossReferences.note: The first vision's horses 'patrolled the earth' and found it 'at rest and tranquil.' The two scenes frame the whole night, and the contrast between the nations' rest and the rest of God's Spirit is the way the cycle closes.

God scattered his people 'like the four winds of heaven' and calls them to flee the land of the north. The four winds and the north return in chapter 6, where the same image becomes God's agents going out, and the north is the place of their last report.
'Disaster from the north will be poured out on all who live in the land.' The north is the standing direction of Babylonian threat, so rest in the north means that threat has been dealt with.

The sons of God present themselves before the LORD, and Satan reports he has been 'walking back and forth' on the earth. The same two verbs of presenting and ranging appear in the chariot vision, which shows the heavenly court in its more orderly and unmistakably holy form.

God makes the clouds his chariot, walks on the wings of the wind, and makes the winds his messengers. The psalm explains why winds, spirits and chariots can be one thing in Zechariah: creation is the equipment of God's court.
'The chariots of God are tens of thousands.' The multitude of heavenly chariots answers the human empire's cavalry. Zechariah shows only four, but the psalm shows how many more stand behind them.

Elisha prays that his servant's eyes be opened, and the hills are full of horses and chariots of fire. Zechariah's vision is the same kind of gift: eyes opened on what already surrounds the people of God.

'When My anger is spent and I have vented My wrath against them, I will be appeased.' This shows the verb behind the rest of God's Spirit in the north, which can describe wrath satisfied, so Zechariah 6:8 can be read as an end of judgment.

Four horses of four colours go out when the Lamb opens the seals. The shared number and colours suggest a connection, but the riders and their missions differ. The passage shows how later Scripture takes up Zechariah's image without simply repeating it.

'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me.' The Lordship over the whole earth that Zechariah's chariots serve is placed in the hands of the risen Jesus, who sends out his disciples to every nation.

Quoting Psalm 104, the writer says God 'makes His angels winds, His servants flames of fire.' This supports reading Zechariah's 'spirits' as winds and servants at once, and it sets those servants beneath the Son.

study.oneStory:
At the beginning of the Bible, God gives the earth to humanity to rule and fill. By Genesis 11 the nations are scattered over the face of the earth, and their rulers rise and fall in the pages that follow. The question the exiles faced was whether those nations were running the story. The last night vision answers that the earth has always had a Lord, that every direction is within his reach, and that his agents go where he sends them. It is a statement of where creation stands: under a King, even when the throne is hidden.

The vision looks backward to the exile. God had used Babylon to judge his people, Jeremiah 25 and 29:10, and then used Persia to let them go. The north's rest is the close of that chapter. It looks forward as well. The prophet's next paragraph sets the Branch on a throne, Zechariah 6:12-13, and later chapters show a king coming on a donkey, 9:9, a pierced one mourned, 12:10, and the LORD becoming king over all the earth, 14:9. The chariots are the first move in that sequence: the throne is secure before the king appears.

In the New Testament this security is not replaced but filled out. Jesus rises, and all authority is his, Matthew 28:18. The church is sent into every direction with the news that the Lord of all the earth has a name. Unlike Zechariah's chariots, which patrol and report, the church goes with a gospel. The story shows the same God in two dispositions, ruling by command in Zechariah and ruling through the cross and the Spirit in the Gospels. Between them the people of God live in a world where the news is still mixed and the throne is still hidden.

The story ends with the rest the vision names. The Lamb stands at the centre of the throne, with the seven Spirits of God 'sent out into all the earth,' Revelation 5:6. The nations bring their glory into the city, Revelation 21:24-26, and there is no more curse, Revelation 22:3. There the chariots have no need to patrol, because nothing remains to be inspected and put right. The Spirit that Zechariah heard was given rest in the north is finally at rest among a people who are at rest with him, in a creation entirely under the Lord of all the earth.

quiz.q: What are the four chariots identified as?

options.text: The four spirits or winds of heaven, sent out from before the Lord of all the earth.
options.note: The angel names them the four spirits of heaven going forth from their station.

options.text: Four human armies of the nations.
options.note: They are heavenly agents, not merely earthly armies.

options.text: The four seasons of the year.
options.note: They are God's agents patrolling the earth, not calendar markers.

options.text: Decorative images with no meaning.
options.note: The angel gives them a clear meaning as God's heavenly agents.

quiz.q: What is the climax of the vision in verse 8?

options.text: Those going north give rest to God's Spirit, His purpose against the oppressor accomplished.
options.note: The north, land of Babylon, is where God's Spirit is given rest.

options.text: The chariots return home defeated.
options.note: The opposite: they accomplish God's purpose and bring rest, not defeat.

options.text: The horses refuse to obey.
options.note: They eagerly go and patrol at the LORD's command.

options.text: Nothing significant happens.
options.note: The rest given to God's Spirit is the whole point of the vision.

quiz.q: How does this vision relate to the first night vision?

options.text: It matches and completes it, framing all eight visions with patrols of the earth.
options.note: The first vision surveyed the earth; this one shows God's rule executed over it.

options.text: It cancels the first vision.
options.note: It completes rather than cancels the opening vision.

options.text: It has no relation to the other visions.
options.note: It is deliberately paired with the first as a bookend.

options.text: It repeats the first with no development.
options.note: It advances from survey to the execution of God's rule and rest.

quiz.q: What does the vision teach about God?

options.text: He is Lord of all the earth, ruling the nations in every direction from His throne.
options.note: The chariots go out from before the Lord of all the earth.

options.text: He controls only the land of Israel.
options.note: His rule reaches every direction of the whole earth.

options.text: He leaves history to chance.
options.note: His agents go only where He commands, so nothing is left to chance.

options.text: He is unaware of what the nations do.
options.note: His chariots patrol and report the whole earth to Him.

quiz.q: How does the vision point to Christ?

options.text: The Lord who commands the chariots is the throne now shared by the risen Christ, ruling the nations.
options.note: All authority in heaven and on earth is given to Christ, Matthew 28:18.

options.text: It shows Christ has no authority over history.
options.note: The opposite: the risen Christ reigns over the nations.

options.text: It teaches the chariots are more powerful than God.
options.note: The chariots serve God's command; they are His agents, not His rivals.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ.
options.note: It points to the risen Christ enthroned as Lord of all the earth.

questions: God's chariots patrol every direction of the earth. How does it steady you to know that no event in the world falls outside His command?
The north, land of the great enemy, was brought under God's judgment. What enemy or fear feels beyond your control that God has already dealt with?
God's Spirit was given rest when His purpose was accomplished. Where do you need to rest in God's finished work rather than striving in your own?
The risen Christ now reigns as Lord of all the earth. How should His rule over the nations shape the way you read the news and pray for the world?
The horses were eager to go at the LORD's word. What is God sending you to do that you have been slow to obey?

translationNotes.note: Four spirits of heaven can also be rendered four winds of heaven; the Hebrew ruach means both, and the same word names God's Spirit given rest in verse 8.
The one with the white horses toward the west can also be read the one with the white horses after them; the directional scheme is debated, but the sweep covers the whole earth.
The land of the north is the direction of Babylon and of the exile; rest to My Spirit signals that God's righteous purpose against the oppressor is accomplished.
